common_name: Iolanthe Magnolia (Large Soft Pink New Zealand Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Iolanthe flowers abundantly even on young trees only a few years old.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving Iolanthe plenty of room to grow into a substantial specimen tree. Bred in New Zealand by Felix Jury from a cross of Magnolia x soulangeana 'Lennei' and his own hybrid 'Mark Jury', Iolanthe produces huge, bowl-shaped flowers up to 10 inches across, soft pink on the outside and creamy white within, opening from distinctive furry gray buds on bare branches in early to mid spring. It flowers profusely even on young trees, and its vigorous, rounded canopy eventually becomes one of the larger hybrid magnolias in cultivation. Along with the deep-red 'Vulcan', Iolanthe is one of the two parents of the dark-flowered hybrid 'Black Tulip', and like other Jury magnolias it performs best where mild, temperate spring conditions reduce the risk of frost damage to open flowers.
sources: Tikorangi: The Jury Garden plant records

common_name: Prolifera Echeveria (Carpet Echeveria, Offsetting Wax Agave)

planting.note: Detach rooted offsets in spring and pot into gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Prolifera forms a spreading mat of rosettes over time, since it is among the most freely offsetting of all agavoides cultivars.

directions: Grow in full sun in fast-draining, mineral-heavy succulent mix, letting the soil dry completely between waterings. First documented in the Mexico City garden of Christian Halbinger and later formally described from cultivation, Prolifera is a lime-green Echeveria agavoides selection whose stemless rosettes bear thick, pointed leaves edged in reddish-pink with a darker terminal spine, the color deepening under bright, cool conditions. True to its name, it offsets prolifically around the base of each rosette, quickly forming a dense mat or carpet rather than the more solitary habit typical of the species. Urn-shaped, peach-red flowers with orange interiors rise on slender stalks in spring, and the cultivar has since been used as a breeding parent, including in the larger-rosetted hybrid 'Frank Reinelt'.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant rooted cane cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger has passed in bright, indirect light with some morning sun tolerated; give this upright cane-type begonia room to grow into a tall, multi-stemmed specimen.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light to partial shade in humus-rich, well-drained potting mix, watering deeply and then letting the top of the mix dry before watering again. Torch is a classic angel-wing cane begonia grown for its glossy, olive-green, silver-spotted leaves with deep red undersides and for pendulous clusters of orange-red flowers that appear over a long season from spring through fall. Upright, jointed canes can reach several feet with staking, forming a full, architectural houseplant or shade-container specimen where a full-size angel wing begonia is wanted. It has been used as a parent in later shrub-type hybrids, including 'Don Miller' and 'Maurice Amey', both bred from crosses involving 'Torch'. Pinch young canes to encourage branching, and repot only when clearly rootbound, since cane begonias flower best when slightly potbound.
sources: American Begonia Society cane-type begonia records

common_name: In Reverse Bearded Iris (Reverse Blue Amoena Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; In Reverse is a modern reverse-amoena Tall Bearded iris later used as a breeding parent, including for the 2004 Dykes Medal winner 'Crowned Heads'.

directions: Hybridized by Keith Keppel, In Reverse is a striking reverse blue amoena bearded iris with deep Colombian-blue standards over much paler, near-white to pale blue-violet falls — essentially the inverse of the classic amoena pattern, in which the falls are usually the darker segment. The heavily ruffled, substantial petals carry a light, sweet fragrance, and the tall, well-branched stalks hold the flowers well above the foliage fan in midseason. In Reverse was later used as a parent in Keppel's own reverse-neglecta introduction 'Crowned Heads', which combined it with 'Honky Tonk Blues' to win the 2004 American Dykes Medal. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting vigorous outer fans in full sun and sharply drained soil.

common_name: Wild Mustang Bearded Iris (Grape-and-Blue-Violet Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Wild Mustang is a mid-20th-century Tall Bearded iris later used as a breeding grandparent of 'Brown Lasso,' the first Border Bearded iris to win the American Dykes Medal.

directions: Hybridized by Z.G. Benson and registered in 1965, Wild Mustang is a Tall Bearded iris with smooth, conical, grape-to-plum-colored standards over lighter blue-violet falls edged in a matching grape-violet border that fades into a dark brown haft, giving each flower a distinctive layered, autumnal color blend. It earned a High Commendation the year of its introduction and an Honorable Mention from the American Iris Society two years later. A cross between Wild Mustang and 'Milestone' produced a seedling that was later combined with 'Punchline' to create the 1981 American Dykes Medal-winning Border Bearded iris 'Brown Lasso'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigorous flowering.
